0.title: One Bible, Two Readings
0.essay:
Jews and Christians hold the same Hebrew Scriptures in their hands. Jesus and his apostles read them, prayed them and preached from them. Yet the two communities read many of their best-known passages in very different ways.

The same book, two readings

When a Christian reads Isaiah 53, he sees the cross. When a Jewish friend reads the same chapter, he will most likely see the sufferings of the Jewish people. When a Christian reads Psalm 22, he hears Jesus crying from the cross. His friend hears David, or Israel in exile. Both are reading carefully. Both love the text. Neither is being foolish.

This study sets the two readings side by side, passage by passage. It aims to describe Jewish interpretation fairly, so that a Jewish reader would recognise his own view. It also explains, without hiding anything, why Christians read these passages as pointing to Jesus of Nazareth. This study’s own conviction, and this commentary’s, is that Jesus is the promised Messiah, and that there is salvation in no one else, for Jew and Gentile alike (Acts 4:12; Romans 1:16). That conviction is held with humility, and with love for the people of whom Jesus said, “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). And it aims to help the reader talk with Jewish friends honestly and kindly.

The units

Reading the Same Scriptures; The Promise in Genesis; Sacrifice, Atonement and the Suffering Servant; The Coming King; The Pierced One and the Two Comings; and Talking with Jewish Friends.

1.title: Reading the Same Scriptures
1.essay:
Before we compare readings of particular verses, we need to see how each community reads the Bible as a whole. Jews and Christians do not only disagree about a handful of prophecies. They come to the same pages through different doors.

The Tanakh and the oral tradition

Jewish people call the Hebrew Bible the Tanakh, a word made from the first letters of its three parts: the Torah (the Law, the five books of Moses), the Nevi’im (the Prophets) and the Ketuvim (the Writings). The books are those of the Protestant Old Testament, in a different order.

In rabbinic Judaism, which is the mainstream of Jewish faith since the destruction of the Temple in AD 70, the written Torah is never read alone. It comes with the oral Torah, the tradition of interpretation believed to have been handed down from Moses. That tradition was written down in the Mishnah (about AD 200) and then discussed at length in the Talmud, the great collection of rabbinic teaching and debate on the Mishnah, completed in Babylonia around AD 500 to 600. Alongside it stand the collections of Midrash, rabbinic commentary on the biblical text, often in the form of sermons, stories and word studies. There are also the Targums, ancient Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Scriptures, made for synagogue hearers who no longer spoke Hebrew well.

Then come the great medieval commentators, still printed around the text in Jewish Bibles today. They include Rashi (eleventh-century France), the best loved, clear and brief; Abraham ibn Ezra (twelfth-century Spain), a careful grammarian; David Kimchi (Provence, around 1200), who often answered Christian interpretations directly; and Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the greatest legal scholar and philosopher of medieval Judaism.

So a Jewish friend reads a verse within this long, living conversation, through centuries of trusted teachers. A Christian who expects him to see Jesus at once has not yet understood that.

The Messiah in Jewish expectation

The hope of the Messiah (the Hebrew word means “anointed one”) is part of traditional Jewish faith. Maimonides listed belief in the Messiah’s coming among his thirteen principles of faith, and many Jews still pray daily for his coming. But the Messiah of mainstream Jewish expectation is a human king from the line of David, not a divine figure.

Maimonides set out the criteria in his law code, the Mishneh Torah (Laws of Kings, chapter 11). The Messiah will be a king from the house of David, devoted to the Torah, who leads Israel to keep it and fights the battles of the Lord. If he succeeds, rebuilds the Temple and gathers the scattered people of Israel, he is certainly the Messiah. Maimonides adds that the Messiah need not perform miracles. Measured by those criteria, Jesus did not rebuild the Temple, gather the exiles or bring peace to the world, so for most Jews the question is closed before it is opened.

How the apostles read the same Scriptures

The first Christians were Jews, and they read the same Scriptures in the same synagogues. What changed their reading was not a new method but a person. After his resurrection Jesus walked with two disciples to Emmaus, “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). That evening he told the eleven that “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). Notice that he named the three parts of the Tanakh.

The apostles followed his lead. When the Ethiopian official asked about Isaiah 53, “Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus” (Acts 8:35). Peter says that the prophets themselves “searched and inquired carefully” about the salvation they foretold, because the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing to “the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (1 Peter 1:10–11).

The Christian claim is not that Jesus is hidden in odd corners of the text, but that the whole story of Israel, its covenants, its sacrifices, its kings and its sufferings, finds its goal in him. Christians read the Old Testament backwards from the empty tomb, as the apostles did. Jewish readers fairly point out that this reading starts from a conviction about Jesus. Christians answer that Jesus himself taught it, and the resurrection is the reason to hold it.

An honest word about the church’s sins

No Christian can talk about this subject honestly without facing the history. For many centuries Jewish people suffered at the hands of people who called themselves Christians. Jews were called “Christ-killers”. Crusaders massacred Jewish communities in the Rhineland in 1096. Jews were expelled from England in 1290 and from Spain in 1492. The lie that Jews murdered Christian children for their blood led to killings across Europe. Jews were shut in ghettos and forced to listen to conversion sermons. Martin Luther, whom Protestants honour for much, wrote bitterly against the Jews late in his life. And the Holocaust took place in the heart of a Europe that called itself Christian.

None of this was faithful to Christ, who was himself a Jew and who prayed for those who crucified him. Paul, a Jew, wrote that he had “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” for his people (Romans 9:2), and warned Gentile believers, “do not be arrogant toward the branches” (Romans 11:18). For many Jews the name of Jesus is tied to this history, and a Christian who would speak of him must first hear that, grieve it and own it without excuses. Our tone matters, because we are saved by grace and not by any superiority of our own.

2.title: The Promise in Genesis
2.essay:
The Bible’s first book is full of promises: an offspring who will crush the serpent, a family through whom the nations will be blessed, a king from the tribe of Judah. Jews and Christians both treasure these chapters. They differ over where the promises lead.

The woman’s offspring (Genesis 3:15)

After the fall, God tells the serpent that the woman’s offspring will bruise its head, while it bruises his heel. Most Jewish interpreters read this as a picture of the lasting struggle between humanity and evil, or between people and the snake: the snake strikes at the heel, and people strike back at its head. Rabbinic tradition often connects the serpent with the evil inclination, the pull towards sin inside every person. Some of the Aramaic Targums, however, link the healing of this wound with the days of the King Messiah, so a messianic reading is not foreign to Jewish tradition.

Christians have long called this verse the first announcement of the gospel. The word “offspring” can be collective, but here one person deals the decisive blow, and the rest of Scripture narrows the line until it reaches one man. Paul alludes to it when he promises that “the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). At the cross the serpent struck the heel of Jesus, and in that very death its head was crushed (Hebrews 2:14).

The blessing of Abraham (Genesis 12:3)

God promised Abraham that “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). In Jewish reading this is the calling of Israel: through Abraham’s descendants, the knowledge of the one true God, his Torah and his justice would come to the world. Many Jews speak of Israel as a light to the nations in this sense, and they can rightly point out that the world’s knowledge of the God of Abraham came through them.

Christians agree, and go further. Paul says that “the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8). The blessing reaches the nations through one descendant of Abraham in particular, “who is Christ” (Galatians 3:16). Today people from every nation worship the God of Abraham because of Jesus. Christians see that as the promise being kept.

Melchizedek

Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, appears briefly in Genesis 14 to bless Abraham, then vanishes. Rabbinic tradition often identifies him with Shem, the son of Noah. The Letter to the Hebrews, written to Jewish believers, reads him differently. Because Scripture gives him no genealogy, he becomes a picture of a priesthood that does not depend on descent from Levi, and a psalm of David promises a king who is “a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). In Jesus, a king from Judah is also a priest who lives for ever (Hebrews 7).

The binding of Isaac

Few stories matter more in Jewish thought than Genesis 22, which Jews call the Akedah, Hebrew for “binding”. God tested Abraham, telling him to offer Isaac, “your only son Isaac, whom you love” (Genesis 22:2). At the last moment the angel stopped him and a ram was offered instead.

In Judaism the Akedah is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, and many prayer books include it in the daily morning prayers. The ram’s horn blown at the New Year recalls the ram caught in the thicket. Rabbinic tradition stresses Isaac’s willing part: in many retellings he is a grown man who freely lets himself be bound. Jews pray that God will remember the binding of Isaac and show mercy to his descendants. The story is also read as God’s final rejection of child sacrifice, and as the supreme example of faithful obedience.

A Christian can honour all of this. He also sees more. Abraham said, “God will provide for himself the lamb” (Genesis 22:8), and the place was named “The LORD will provide” (Genesis 22:14). That mountain, Moriah, is where the Temple later stood (2 Chronicles 3:1). Isaac was spared, but centuries later, in the same city, God did what he did not ask of Abraham. “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32) is Paul’s echo of this chapter. The beloved son carried the wood up the hill; the beloved Son carried his cross. The Jewish sense that God shows mercy because of a binding long ago is, Christians believe, nearer the truth than many realise.

The sceptre of Judah (Genesis 49:10)

Dying Jacob says that “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet” (Genesis 49:10), until a mysterious word in the Hebrew, Shiloh, is fulfilled. The ESV renders it “until tribute comes to him”; others read “until he comes to whom it belongs”, or take Shiloh as the town where the tabernacle stood.

Here the older Jewish tradition and the Christian reading stand close together. The ancient Targums render the line with words about the coming of the Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs, and Rashi himself follows them in reading it of King Messiah. Many modern Jewish interpreters prefer other readings, often of David’s rise or of the town of Shiloh. Christians read the verse of Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5), to whom “shall be the obedience of the peoples” (Genesis 49:10). People of every nation now bow to a king from Judah. That, Christians believe, is the obedience the verse foresaw.

3.title: Sacrifice, Atonement and the Suffering Servant
3.essay:
Sacrifice runs through the Torah, from the Passover lamb to the Day of Atonement. For nearly two thousand years there has been no Temple and no altar. How Jews and Christians answer the question “What happened to sacrifice?” lies near the heart of their difference.

Passover and the Day of Atonement

At the first Passover each household killed a lamb and put its blood on the doorposts. God said, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). Jewish families still keep the Passover meal, the Seder, retelling the story of freedom from Egypt. Since the Temple fell no lamb is sacrificed; a roasted bone on the Seder plate recalls it.

On the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, the high priest entered the Most Holy Place with blood, and laid the people’s sins on the head of a goat that was sent away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21). The Torah grounds this in a principle: “it is the blood that makes atonement by the life” (Leviticus 17:11). Yom Kippur is still the most solemn day of the Jewish year, given to fasting, confession and prayer.

Atonement in Judaism after the Temple

When the Romans destroyed the Temple in AD 70, the sacrifices stopped. The rabbis taught that God had not left his people without a way back. A well-known rabbinic story tells of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, the leader of the generation, comforting a disciple who mourned the lost altar: acts of loving-kindness, he said, now atone as the sacrifices did, and he cited Hosea: “For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

So in mainstream Judaism atonement rests on repentance (teshuvah, turning back to God), prayer and charitable deeds. The High Holy Day prayers say that these three avert the severity of God’s decree. Prayer is offered in place of the Temple sacrifices, and Yom Kippur itself, joined with sincere repentance, brings forgiveness. The Mishnah adds that wrongs done to another person are not forgiven on Yom Kippur until the wrongdoer has put things right with the one he wronged. Jewish teaching also rejects the idea that one person can die for the sins of another; each person answers for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:20).

A Christian should take this seriously. The prophets did value a broken heart above burnt offerings (Psalm 51:17), and Jesus himself quoted Hosea 6:6. But Christians also notice that the Torah gave Israel sacrifice as God’s appointed way of atonement, and that the prophets who called for repentance never declared sacrifice abolished. The New Testament answers the question differently: the sacrifices did not simply end, they were fulfilled. “It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). They pointed to one who “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood” (Hebrews 9:12). John the Baptist called Jesus “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), and Paul wrote, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Jesus died at Passover, and within a generation the Temple was gone.

The servant of Isaiah 52:13–53:12

No passage is discussed more between Jews and Christians. A servant of the Lord is “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3). “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). He dies, is buried “with a rich man in his death” (Isaiah 53:9), and yet “he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days” (Isaiah 53:10).

The older Jewish reading was often messianic. The Targum of Isaiah, known as Targum Jonathan, opens the passage with the words “my servant, the Messiah”, though it then applies much of the suffering to Israel or to the nations rather than to the Messiah himself. Some rabbinic texts also speak of the Messiah bearing sickness and suffering in the words of Isaiah 53.

From the Middle Ages the reading that became dominant was different. Rashi read the servant as the people of Israel, and many later Jewish commentators followed him. In this view the speakers in chapter 53 are the nations, who at last realise that the Jewish people they despised were suffering righteously, and even bearing the consequences of the nations’ own sins. Jewish readers point out that Isaiah does call Israel God’s servant: “You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified” (Isaiah 49:3). Given the centuries of Jewish suffering, often at Christian hands, a Christian should hear this reading with sympathy, not scorn.

Why Christians read it of Jesus

Christians give several reasons. In Isaiah the servant is sometimes Israel the nation, often failing and in need of rescue. But in chapter 49 the servant is also given a mission to Israel, “to raise up the tribes of Jacob” (Isaiah 49:6), so he cannot simply be Israel. The servant of chapter 53 is innocent: “he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth” (Isaiah 53:9). He suffers not for his own sins but “for the transgression of my people” (Isaiah 53:8), and the prophet’s people is Israel. And his suffering is willing and saving: “he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).

The New Testament reads the chapter of Jesus again and again (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:22–25). Here is one who was rejected, killed alongside criminals, buried in a rich man’s tomb, raised to life, and is now honoured by many nations. Christians believe the passage describes him as no one else in history fits. The innocent one bore what the guilty deserved, and so the guilty go free.

4.title: The Coming King
4.essay:
The hope of a coming king is where Jewish and Christian readings agree most. Both expect a son of David who will reign in justice. They disagree about who he is, what kind of king he is, and whether he has come.

The promise to David (2 Samuel 7)

God promised David a house, a line of kings, and said of his son, “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). This promise is the root of Jewish messianic hope: the Messiah is the son of David who restores David’s throne. Christians share that root completely. The New Testament opens with “Jesus Christ, the son of David” (Matthew 1:1), and the angel promised Mary that God would give her son “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32).

The difference is in what “forever” requires. Jewish readers expect a human king reigning in Jerusalem, followed by his descendants. Christians believe the promise is kept more fully than David could have imagined: by a son of David who rose from the dead and so reigns for ever himself.

Psalms 2 and 110

Psalm 2 speaks of the Lord’s anointed king, to whom God says, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). In Jewish reading this is the language of royal adoption, spoken over David or a king of his line at his anointing. Rabbinic tradition also read it of the Messiah, son of David, to whom God will give the nations.

Psalm 110 begins, “The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1). Rabbinic tradition often applied this psalm to Abraham, and many Jewish interpreters read it of David, as a court singer speaking of his king. Jesus asked the teachers of his day how David could call his own son “Lord” (Matthew 22:41–46), and no one could answer. The New Testament quotes it more than any other Old Testament verse: the Messiah enthroned beside God, a king who is also a priest for ever (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 1:13).

Isaiah’s child and branch (Isaiah 7, 9 and 11)

Isaiah 7:14 promises Ahaz a sign: a young woman will bear a son called Immanuel, “God with us”. The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and Jewish readers point out, fairly, that it does not in itself mean a virgin. They read the sign as a child born in Ahaz’s own day, perhaps Hezekiah or a son of Isaiah. Christians agree that the sign spoke to Ahaz’s day. But the Greek translation made by Jews before Christ used the word for virgin, Matthew followed it (Matthew 1:23), and the name Immanuel is taken up in chapters 8 and 9 in ways that reach beyond any ordinary child.

Isaiah 9:6 says that “to us a child is born, to us a son is given”, and calls him “Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). Many Jewish interpreters, from rabbinic times, identified the child as Hezekiah, and read most of the titles as describing God, who gives the child his name, rather than the child himself. Christians answer that the same title, “mighty God”, is used of the Lord himself in the next chapter (Isaiah 10:21), and that the child’s kingdom has “no end” (Isaiah 9:7), which no reign of Hezekiah fulfilled.

Isaiah 11 describes “a shoot from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1), filled with the Spirit, judging the poor with righteousness, when “the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (Isaiah 11:9). Jews and Christians both read this of the Messiah. Jewish readers take it as proof that the Messiah has not yet come. Christians believe the shoot has sprung up, and that the full picture will be seen when he comes again.

Bethlehem, the donkey and the Branch

Micah 5:2 promises a ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah, “whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days” (Micah 5:2). The Targum on Micah reads it of the Messiah, and in Matthew’s Gospel the chief priests and scribes of Herod’s day pointed to it without hesitation (Matthew 2:4–6). Jewish readers take “from of old” to mean the ancient line of David; Christians hear in it a hint of the one who existed before he was born.

Zechariah 9:9 announces a king coming to Jerusalem “humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9), and rabbinic tradition read this of the Messiah too. Jesus deliberately fulfilled it on the way to his death. Jeremiah promises a righteous Branch for David whose name will be “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6). Jewish interpreters take this as a name that praises God; Christians believe it describes what Christ is for his people.

The son of man (Daniel 7:13–14)

In Daniel’s vision, “with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man” (Daniel 7:13), and he receives an everlasting kingdom. Many Jewish interpreters read this figure as a symbol of Israel, the faithful people, since the chapter later speaks of the kingdom given to the saints. But some rabbinic sources read it of the Messiah. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) sets this verse beside Zechariah 9:9 and asks how the Messiah can come both with the clouds and on a donkey. Its answer: if Israel is worthy, he comes with the clouds of heaven; if not, lowly and riding on a donkey.

Christians find this striking, because the New Testament says he comes in both ways. He came first on a donkey. At his trial, he told the high priest that they would see “the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62). The humble king and the king of glory are one person.

5.title: The Pierced One and the Two Comings
5.essay:
Some of the passages Christians treasure most speak of one who suffers, is pierced and is mourned. Jewish readers ask a hard question in reply: if Jesus was the Messiah, where is the peace the prophets promised? This unit takes both seriously.

Psalm 22

Psalm 22 opens with the cry Jesus prayed from the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1). It goes on to describe mockers, bones out of joint, a parched tongue and clothes divided by lot. Then it turns to praise, and ends with the hope that “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD” (Psalm 22:27).

In Jewish reading the psalm is David’s lament, or the voice of Israel suffering in exile, which God at last delivers. Christians agree that David wrote from his own suffering. But Christians notice that the details go beyond anything recorded of David, and that the ending is out of proportion to one man’s rescue: because of this sufferer’s deliverance, the nations turn to God. Jesus took the opening words on his lips at the cross, and the Gospel writers saw the rest of the psalm fulfilled around him (Matthew 27:35, 39–46; John 19:23–24).

Verse 16 has a well-known textual question, and it is best stated plainly. Most Hebrew manuscripts read “like a lion, my hands and feet”. The ancient Greek translation, made by Jews before the time of Christ, and other early versions read “they have pierced” (or “dug”), as do some Hebrew manuscripts, and a Psalms scroll from the Judean desert appears to support a verb rather than “like a lion”. The ESV prints “they have pierced my hands and feet”. Jewish readers often regard this as a Christian alteration; the evidence shows that the reading existed among Jews before Christians used it. A Christian need not win the argument to read the psalm of Christ. Even on the other reading the hands and feet are the point, and the rest of the psalm stands on its own.

The one they pierced (Zechariah 12:10)

God promises to pour out on Jerusalem “a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that, when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10). Many Jewish interpreters read the verse as Israel looking to God because of those of their people whom the nations had killed in battle, and mourning for them.

The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) records a discussion of this verse. One rabbi said the mourning is over the evil inclination, which will be slain in the age to come. Another said it is over the Messiah son of Joseph, who will be killed. In rabbinic tradition, the Messiah son of Joseph is a warrior Messiah from the tribe of Joseph who falls in battle before the Messiah son of David comes to reign. So the idea of a slain Messiah, mourned by Israel, is not a Christian invention. It appears in Jewish tradition itself.

Christians notice that the speaker is God himself (“when they look on me”), and yet the one pierced is “him”. John saw the verse fulfilled at the cross (John 19:37), and Revelation looks ahead to the day when “every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Revelation 1:7). Where rabbinic tradition spoke of two Messiahs, one who dies and one who reigns, Christians see one Messiah who comes twice.

Daniel’s seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24–27)

Daniel 9 speaks of seventy “weeks”, periods of seven years, after which God will “put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness” (Daniel 9:24). Then “an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing” (Daniel 9:26), and the city and sanctuary will be destroyed. Jewish interpreters have usually read the anointed one as a high priest or ruler of the Second Temple period, and the destruction as the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or as the events under Antiochus Epiphanes in the second century BC.

The chronology is difficult, and Christians differ about it too. But they have long seen here the death of Jesus, cut off with nothing, followed within a generation by the destruction of the city and the Temple. If an anointed one was to be cut off before the Second Temple fell, the question “Who was he?” deserves an answer.

“But where is the peace?”

This is the strongest Jewish objection. The prophets promised that in the Messiah’s days “nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore” (Isaiah 2:4). Two thousand years after Jesus, wars continue, and Jewish people have suffered terribly, often in his name. By Maimonides’ standard, Jesus has not done what the Messiah must do.

A Christian should not brush this aside. The answer of the New Testament is that the Messiah comes twice. He came first to suffer and to deal with sin, the deepest cause of all war. He will come again to bring the peace of his kingdom to the whole earth. “Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him” (Hebrews 9:28). The suffering comes first, then the glory (Luke 24:26).

Meanwhile the peace has begun. Christ “himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), joining Jew and Gentile into one people, and the knowledge of the God of Israel has already spread to the ends of the earth. That is not yet the whole of what the prophets promised. It is the first fruits of it, and the pledge that the rest will come.

6.title: Talking with Jewish Friends
6.essay:
Many Christians with Jewish friends or colleagues have never talked with them about Jesus, afraid of giving offence or unsure where to start. This unit offers some help, beginning with the objections a Jewish friend may raise.

“We believe in one God”

The heart of Jewish prayer is the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Many Jews hear the Christian doctrine of the Trinity as a belief in three gods, and the worship of Jesus as the worship of a man. To a Jew that is idolatry, and many have died rather than commit it.

The honest answer begins by agreeing. Christians believe the Shema with all their hearts; Jesus called it the first commandment (Mark 12:29). The Trinity is not three gods but one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Explain that Christians did not add a second god to the God of Israel. They came to this belief because the first Jewish believers, who would never have worshipped a man, met in Jesus the God of Israel himself, “and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Be patient: your friend’s concern for God’s oneness is one you share.

“Jesus did not fulfil the prophecies”

Your friend may say that Jesus did not rebuild the Temple, gather the exiles or bring world peace. The Christian answer is the two comings: the Messiah first came to suffer for sin, as Isaiah 53 and Zechariah 12 foresaw, and he will come again in glory. It helps to admit that the Christian reading depends on the resurrection. If Jesus did not rise, Christians are wrong. If he did, the whole picture changes. Invite your friend to look at the evidence for that, and to read the Gospels for himself, which many Jews have never done.

“What about the Law?”

Jewish life is shaped by the Torah, and many Jews think Christians dismiss it. Again, begin by agreeing. Jesus said, “I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). The Law is holy, and Christians read it as God’s word. But Christians believe that no one has ever kept it perfectly, and that the Law itself pointed to a righteousness given by God. Paul says that the righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, “although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it” (Romans 3:21). Jesus kept the Law perfectly in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours when we trust him (Romans 5:19). This is not an escape from God’s commands. It is the new covenant Jeremiah promised, when God writes his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–33).

“Your people persecuted mine”

This may be the hardest objection of all, and it is not an argument but a wound. Do not defend what cannot be defended. Say plainly that what was done to Jewish people in the name of Christ was evil and a betrayal of him. Then point gently to Jesus, a Jew who wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). Many Jewish people have never been shown that the Jesus of the Gospels is not the Jesus of the persecutors.

What we share

Christians and Jews share far more than either often realises: one God, the Creator; the Hebrew Scriptures as God’s word; the patriarchs; the Ten Commandments; the call to justice and mercy; the hope of a coming kingdom of peace; and the resurrection of the dead. Paul lists Israel’s gifts with love: “to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises” (Romans 9:4). And Jesus himself is “from their race, according to the flesh” (Romans 9:5).

Romans 9 to 11

Paul wrote these chapters with tears. He wished himself cut off from Christ for his people’s sake (Romans 9:3). He asked, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1). He said that a partial hardening has come upon Israel “until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26). Christians understand that verse in different ways. This commentary holds, humbly, that Paul expects a future turning of the Jewish people as a whole to Christ, by faith in him as the Deliverer, before he returns. It is not a separate way of salvation, and it is not a political programme. It is God’s mercy, and it should make Gentile believers humble, not proud (Romans 11:18–20). Paul ends not with a timetable but with worship: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33).

Practical guidance

  • Listen first. Ask your friend what he believes and what his faith means to him. Jewish people are as varied as Christians: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, secular. Do not assume.
  • Know your Bible. Read the passages in this study for yourself, in context, and be ready to read them together.
  • Be honest. Admit difficulties, own the church’s sins, and do not claim more than the text says.
  • Never pressure. Conversion is the work of God’s Spirit, not of clever arguments. Answer “with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15).
  • Love. Be a real friend, whether or not he ever agrees with you. Pray for him, as Paul did: “my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved” (Romans 10:1).

We do not speak of Jesus because we are better. We speak because we were outsiders brought near by grace, grafted into Israel’s olive tree (Romans 11:17). The gospel is still “the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). We share it as people who have been shown mercy, with the people to whom the promises first belonged.
